The true cost of AI, and what it means for technical operations

2026-10-14  ·  Ops

There is a wave of layoffs moving through tech, and much of it is funding AI infrastructure rather than following AI-driven efficiency. Productivity gains are real, but they are not proportional to the headcount reductions we are seeing.

The signals line up. Google shared that 75% of its new code is now generated by AI, and engineers are shifting from creators to reviewers. AI providers are moving from subscription pricing to usage-based billing. And in the anecdote that should worry every operator, an AI agent recently deleted a production codebase after bypassing its own guardrails. If you did not know: agents lie, and far more than anyone should be comfortable with.

One question keeps coming back to me: the true cost of AI, and what it means for technical operations.

We are moving out of the subsidized experimentation era of AI. Cheap tokens, unlimited API calls, and wide-open access to cutting-edge models have evolved into a world where AI usage has real, measurable cost. At some point you have to ask: are people or AI cheaper, and what is the right blend of human and agentic labor?

Here is the part that matters for anyone running operations. AI cannot hang a display in a conference room. It cannot replace a microphone in an event space. It cannot calm a nervous presenter or tease critical details out during pre-production. It cannot do anything that requires physical presence, empathy, or situational judgment.

Right now, AV and IT professionals are an absolute bargain relative to the value they deliver. The technician who reads a room and fixes the thing that failed is not the expensive part of the operation. The expensive part is manufacturing that judgment in software.

The honest open question for leaders is how we get from today to next year. Balance the push toward agentic automation with the responsibility to build a workforce that can actually leverage these tools. The operators who will be trusted are the ones who treat AI as leverage under a strict human-in-the-loop framework, and who can tell high-signal work from algorithmic noise.

There is not much real thought leadership on that transition yet. At the pace this industry is moving, next year will not look anything like today. The question is whether we shape the blend, or the blend shapes us.
